Abstract: Power and energy consumption are becoming the most important restrictions on driving computer systems.
Especially, HPC systems still require more performance despite their limited power supply, and it is necessary to ex-
plore methodologies to enhance their performance within this limitation. Approximate computing (AC) is a promising
technique for optimizing the trade-oﬀs among application execution performance, application output correctness, and
power consumption during execution. However, applying AC sometimes causes unexpected eﬀects on the output and
performance due to cache behavior, compiler optimization, and so on. This paper discusses dynamic approximate
computing methods, which enable changing data precision in applications at runtime, for more ﬂexible and eﬀec-
tive approximate computing (AC). This paper also evaluates the beneﬁts and drawbacks of dynamic AC with some
high-performance computing (HPC) applications and workloads.
Keywords: HPC, approximate computing, performance evaluation
1.
Introduction
Improving the performance of computer systems is becom-
ing increasingly challenging due to various limitations, including
memory subsystem bandwidth, network bandwidth/latency, and
the available power budget. Although utilizing domain-speciﬁc
accelerators, such as GPUs and FPGAs, is one of the solutions
to tackle this problem, we still require further improvement in
system performance.
Approximate computing (AC) technique, which optimizes the
trade-oﬀs among data precision, computational performance, and
power consumption, is also one of the promising solutions to
improve performance beyond the given amount of hardware re-
sources. AC techniques will enable us to achieve higher perfor-
mance by reducing data precision for computations in an appli-
cation. However, less data precision will result in less accurate
output from the application and may require additional computa-
tion to achieve the desired accuracy. To optimize and accelerate
accuracy-hungry applications, such as HPC applications, by fully
utilizing AC, there is a need for a dynamic AC technique to ad-
just data precision at runtime, as well as a modeling method to
predict the relationship between performance and data precision
within an application. This control cannot be realized with con-
ventional AC, which applies the same data precision to the whole
application, and dynamic data precision control (transprecision
computation) is essential.
The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 re-
views the related works.
Section 3 introduces our idea about
dynamic approximate computing techniques, rank-level AC and

2.
Related Work
Approximate Computing (AC) can be applied on various levels
in a system, from hardware to application [1], [2], [3]. However,
most of them target applications that are robust against degrada-
tion of calculation precision, such as image processing and deep
learning.
Considering HPC systems, most applications that run on them
require higher precision to obtain accurate results.
AC tech-
niques for applications robust against lower precision computa-
tion will not work well for HPC applications. Hara et al. ac-
celerated HPC applications by oﬄoading some tasks to FPGAs
with various ﬂoating-point data types [4]. Saha et al. proposed
a deadline scheduling method for a real-time system with multi-
core processors. This method resizes the cache size to keep power
consumption below the given budget [5]. Morie et al. proposed
data transfer APIs for MPI communication to enable rank-level
approximate computing, which allows ranks in an application to
be computed with diﬀerent data precision from each other [6].
Related to ﬁne-grained or dynamic AC techniques, there are
various works, especially on the application layer. Ichimura et
al. proposed an acceleration method, that changes the data pre-
cision from lower to higher precision, for preconditioned CG
solvers in an earthquake simulation [7]. Durand et al. proposed
an optimization algorithm for the eﬃcient CG method on a pro-
cessor that supports variable precision computations [8]. Kelley
proposed a CG method that combines various precision compu-
tations [9]. These methods and algorithms succeeded in acceler-
ating the target applications by dynamically adjusting data pre-

3.
Dynamic Approximate Computing
Utilizing the same data precision throughout the entire applica-
tion, namely static AC, is a straightforward way to apply AC for
HPC applications. However, this static method will decrease the
eﬀectiveness of AC, because each application has its own struc-
ture and sensitivities to lower data precision. To overcome the
problem with the static AC, it is required to consider adjusting
data precision at runtime.
As shown in Fig. 1, these dynamic approximate computing
techniques will require us to realize:
• Application analysis to estimate the relationship between
data precision and its performance, and to detect suitable
data precision
• Data transfer optimization to reduce overhead for data preci-
sion adjustment
• System software to detect application structure and to con-
trol data precision at runtime
• Methodologies to utilize accelerators (GPUs, NPUs, FPGAs,
and so on) for various data precision and higher performance
In this paper, we consider data transfer and application struc-
ture for dynamic AC as our fundamentals, because most HPC
users are allowed to optimize their applications at the library and
application layers.
3.1
Approximate Computing for HPC Applications
Especially in HPC applications, to optimize the trade-oﬀbe-
tween computational performance and accuracy more eﬀectively,
it is required to consider which part of the application can be ro-
bust against lower data precision and which synchronization point
has unnecessary wait time due to the load imbalance.
Namely, there are temporal and spatial structures in HPC ap-
plications; When we consider the spatial structure among ranks
or nodes used for executing a target application, we can adjust the
data precision used in each rank. This data precision adjustment

What we need to realize dynamic AC.
will reduce the amount of load imbalance among ranks and nodes
in the application, resulting in improved performance. When we
consider the temporal structure during the runtime of an HPC ap-
plication, various blocks, such as loops, basic blocks, and subrou-
tine/function calls, are executed over time. Additionally, many
HPC applications comprise large main loops for time evolution
or convergence, and each iteration varies in terms of robustness
against smaller precision data.
To enable dynamic approximate computing for HPC applica-
tions, this paper considers both their temporal and spatial struc-
tures.
3.2
Rank-level AC
As written above, to utilize the spatial characteristics of HPC
applications and systems with approximate computing tech-
niques, it is important to enable each rank/process to do com-
putations with diﬀerent data precisions independently. Figure 2
shows an image of rank-level AC [6], [10]. As shown in Fig. 2 a),
some of the MPI applications contain load imbalance, and the
ranks that complete their computation earlier must wait for oth-
ers at the point of barrier synchronization. When it is possible to
allow the ranks to proceed with their computation with diﬀerent
data types, considering their loads, slow ranks can be accelerated
by computing with lower data precision. As a result, synchro-
nization overhead can be reduced and the total performance will
be improved as shown in Fig. 2 b).
However, most HPC applications involve data transfers among
ranks/nodes, and the ordinary MPI speciﬁcation requires both the
data transfer source and destination to communicate using the
same data type. To enable this rank-level AC for HPC applica-
tions with MPI, it is required to extend the underlying data trans-
fer libraries and API to support diﬀerent data types for commu-
nication sources and destinations. In Fig. 2 b), rank i executes its
computation in FP32, and rank j in FP64. It is required to cast or
convert the FP32 data to FP64 to send data from rank i to j, and
vice versa.
Changing data precision during data transfer increases com-
munication overhead. At the same time, data transfer with lower
data precision decreases the overhead. We need to optimize the
trade-oﬀbetween them.

As discussed in Ref. [6], the overhead of converting data pre-

rank, the data transfer cost model will be helpful.
In addition, the target program must be multi-versioned to al-
low each rank to proceed with the computation with its preferred
data precision. This multi-versioning and code instrumentation
to make each rank select its preferred version (or data precision)
can be realized relatively easily by a compiler.
3.4
Iteration-level AC
To obtain more accurate results with HPC applications, we typ-
ically utilize higher-precision data types. However, the higher the
data precision, the longer the execution time. To tackle this prob-
lem, the authors propose iteration-level AC, which utilizes iter-
ations within the main loop of an HPC application. Many HPC
applications consist of main loops for time evolution or conver-
gence. Robustness against lower data precision and its impact on
the ﬁnal computational results of each iteration will vary depend-
ing on the application structure and the progress of the computa-
tion. Especially in applications involving convergent algorithms,
the ﬁrst several iterations play an important role in treating initial
values and stabilizing the data for the following iterations. The
last several iterations will be important to obtaining ﬁnal results
and must be computed with higher precision.
Figure 3 shows an image of iteration-level AC. In the original
application, all iterations are computed with the same data type
(FP64 or higher in many cases). With the proposed iteration-
level AC, the ﬁrst several iterations are computed using higher-
precision data (FP64 in the case of Fig. 3). This makes it possible
Fig. 3
An example of iteration-level AC.
to improve the data accuracy rapidly and stabilize the following
iterations. After that, iterations in the middle can be executed
with lower-precision data (FP32 in the case of Fig. 3) for better
performance. Finally, the last iterations should be executed with
higher-precision data to obtain accurate results. These three steps
make it possible to optimize the trade-oﬀbetween performance
and accuracy.
To optimize the application with this iteration-level AC, the
number of iterations for each step must be adjusted. In addition,
data copy while changing the data precision will be necessary to
realize iteration-level AC. We need to take into account the over-
head of data copying and changing the data types between the
steps in terms of performance and memory footprint.
3.5
Enabling Iteration-level AC
Typical ﬁne-grained AC or transprecision computing tech-
niques require much eﬀort from runtime libraries or application
programmers, as it is necessary to maintain individual threads
or processes to run while changing data precision appropriately.
Such optimization will not be possible without dynamic informa-
tion obtained at runtime or proﬁling data. Then, we consider a
simple method to reduce the cost of proﬁling and programming
applications with AC techniques.
In iteration-level AC, the basic structure of the main loop in
the target application can be kept, but it is multi-versioned with
diﬀerent data precisions. This process can be done by copying
the program structure while changing the data type in the code
segment, and inserting a data copy with a cast. With traditional
compiler techniques, iteration-level AC can be applied easily.
One of the drawbacks of this method is the overhead for data
copy with casting. With simple multi-versioning, explicit data
copy must be inserted at the point to change the data precision.

4.2
Evaluation for Rank-level AC
To evaluate our data transfer APIs and libraries, we employ
ping-pong communication between two nodes. By analyzing data
transfer bandwidth with FP32/FP64 data with and without chang-
ing data precision, it becomes possible to judge whether it is bet-
ter to apply AC to the source/destination ranks or not. This judg-
ment relies on the amount of the data to be transferred, the pre-
cision of the data, the overhead for changing data precision, etc.
Based on this evaluation, a performance model can be obtained
to estimate data transfer overhead for rank-level AC.

To optimize internal buﬀer management, options related to SIMD

Evaluation Results and Discussion
This section summarizes the evaluation results for rank-level
and iteration-level AC, and provides a detailed discussion of
them.
5.1
Evaluation Results for Rank-level AC
To discuss the eﬀectiveness of the proposed data transfer li-
brary for rank-level AC, we evaluated data transfer bandwidth
with varying communication sizes. Based on this bandwidth eval-
uation, we developed a data transfer cost model to estimate the
data transfer overhead required to achieve rank-level AC.

Bandwidth Evaluation with Data Type Convert

the proposed APIs and libraries when converting double/FP64 to

As shown in Fig. 4, data transfer with data type conversion

6.
Conslusions
This paper introduces dynamic and ﬁne-grained approximate
computing (AC) techniques.
Thinking of spatial structure among nodes or ranks, rank-level
AC, which allows each rank to execute its computation with its
appropriate data precision individually, will give us many oppor-
tunities to reduce barrier synchronization overhead. To achieve
the rank-level AC, we need to extend the underlying data transfer
libraries to support changing data precision during data transfer,
which can also reduce data transfer overhead. However, as with
other AC techniques, transferring data with lower precision may
decrease the accuracy of the computation results and may require
additional computation.
Thinking of the temporal structure of an application, iteration-
level AC, which adjusts data precision according to the progress
of computations in units of mail loop iterations within a target
application, will give us more opportunities to apply AC for ac-
celerating its execution. However, we need to consider the num-
ber of iterations executed with lower data precision. If we exceed
the limitation to keep the accuracy of the application’s execution
results, it will not be able to recover even if we increase the data
precision afterward. This means that it is required to realize an
application structure analyzer to detect a part that is robust against
lower data precision, and how much iteration can be executed in
lower data precision while keeping its accuracy.
As our future work, we plan to implement an analyzer to de-
tect a part in an application to apply dynamic and ﬁner-grained
AC into a compiler, and to extend our data transfer API for more
ﬂexible and low-overhead approximate data transfers. This eﬀort
will enable us to realize a more ﬂexible AC, which considers the
hierarchical structure of the target applications. Also, we would
like to develop a compiler framework to automate applying the
proposed dynamic approximate computing methods simultane-
ously.

Abstract: Power and energy consumption are becoming the most important restrictions on driving computer systems. Especially, HPC systems still require more performance despite their limited power supply, and it is necessary to ex- plore methodologies to enhance their performance within this limitation. Approximate computing (AC) is a promising technique for optimizing the trade-oﬀs among application execution performance, application output correctness, and power consumption during execution. However, applying AC sometimes causes unexpected eﬀects on the output and performance due to cache behavior, compiler optimization, and so on. This paper discusses dynamic approximate computing methods, which enable changing data precision in applications at runtime, for more ﬂexible and eﬀec- tive approximate computing (AC). This paper also evaluates the beneﬁts and drawbacks of dynamic AC with some high-performance computing (HPC) applications and workloads.
